The implementation of Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) has been adopted in various 5G systems, and its flexibility and efficiency have driven research into its optimization. Although studies into the performance enhancement of NOMA have produced positive results, researchers are increasingly focusing on the security risks associated with its usage. To address the security concerns, a new framework called Enhanced Deciphering Command (E-DC-FO) was developed, which utilizes machine learning to train a security-aware NOMA framework. In this E-DC-FO framework, the base station employs the entropy of decoded data to filter out erroneous deciphered commands and establishes a secure communication link, while simultaneously optimizing for data transmission efficiency. To reduce the computational load, the use of E-DC-FO can be extended to include local deciphering by user devices, and a scaled version called Deciphering Command with Safeguarded NOMA (DC-SNOMA) is proposed, and its effectiveness compared to existing methods, demonstrating its feasibility in a realistic environment.

We develop a specialized algorithm for finding the principal component in rotationally symmetric distributions by using L1 norm, based on a coordinate transformation. This approach leverages an existing method but adapts it to enhance robustness against outliers while maintaining circular symmetry in data distributions. By incorporating the transformation into the scoring rule, we avoid the inefficiency of converting robust estimates to maximum likelihood ones. Our proposed transformation leads to faster convergence in the expectation maximum likelihood method, potentially skipping the slowly converging step identified in previous studies, and enables sample sizes to be an order of magnitude smaller. Numerical experiments confirm the superior performance of this method in terms of convergence speed and statistical efficiency.

Traditionally, e-commerce platforms match product listings with user queries through keyword matching and semantic tagging methods. However, these approaches fall short in accurately identifying user intent, especially when users express their needs through emotional-driven questions. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel strategy that incorporates the BERT model to refine the semantic tagging process. By combining this new method with a batch of pre-tagged products, we can enhance the matching results between product listings and user questions, demonstrating significant improvements in retrieval effectiveness.

The study of power series in fully ordered groups has long been a topic of interest in the fields of analysis and algebra, especially in relation to solving higher ordered polynomial equations. This research extends previous work by generalizing power series from fully ordered groups to include coefficients from their associated power series. This extension significantly improves the applicability of the theory to solving equations, as demonstrated in related studies. Furthermore, previous limitations on the ordered groups used in this context are surpassed in this research.

Asynchronous polars exhibit a wide range of radio output intensity, which cannot be fully explained by current theoretical models. To gain more insight, researchers are comparing them to normal polars, where the magnetic field is aligned with the white dwarf's rotation axis. By analyzing the X-ray data from 14 asynchronous polars and 31 normal polars, a clear difference in behavior is revealed. The correlation between radio and X-ray signals is evident in the data set of asynchronous polars, in contrast to no such correlation exists for normal polars. Furthermore, there is a clear difference in the average ratio of radio to X-ray outputs, which is significantly higher for normal polars. This comparison provides a new perspective on the conditions required for radio emission to occur.

This introduction to the Reduced Basis Approach for time-dependent Fluid-Structure Interaction Problems is segmented. We outline the basic RBF frameworks, encompassing both the Dirichlet-type and Neumann-type problems. Subsequently, we explore key challenges in applying the RBF methodologies, including the a priori bounds and the non-matching grids phenomenon.

In complex and changing environments, robots often struggle to navigate efficiently and adapt their paths accordingly. To tackle this challenge, researchers have developed hierarchical map representations that provide a structured overview of an environment while maintaining flexibility. This paper presents HiTMap, a novel representation combining a hexagonal grid with a hierarchical structure to depict environments, featuring a compact set of 'high-level' cells connected to detailed 'low-level' cells. HiTMap enables rapid path planning for small changes and more customized approaches through a multi-level A* algorithm, allowing for flexible and efficient navigation. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of HiTMap in providing flexible and efficient path finding and navigation in dynamic and complex environments.

This paper outlines our approach and outcomes for Task 1 of SemEval-2019 Challenge 2019, focused on identifying offensive language in tweets. We participated with two separate entries, contributing 1,210 tests to the shared test set. For Base Model 1, we employed a single classical machine learning algorithm, specifically an SVM, adapted for classifying three categories. For Base Model 2, we utilized a neural network, specifically BERT, also modified for the same three-category classification task. Both models were evaluated using F1-micro scoring, with our approaches achieving 0.20.53 and 0.20.79 respectively.

Employing atomic interferometry in combination with a magnetometer utilizing superconducting materials can sensitively detect minute magnetic field changes within a Meissner layer on the superconducting surface. By taking advantage of the uniformity of this layer and mitigating risks of contamination, one element of two-component atomic interferometry allows for a sensitive measurement of magnetic field alterations specifically confined to a narrow layer, as opposed to traditional two-component methods. Moreover, utilizing a superconducting material reduces magnetometers' susceptibility to contamination by paramagnetic substances, facilitating precise experiments, and is particularly useful in atomic experiments conducted in vacuums with residual gases, or when measuring magnetic substances.

The distinctive properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials have sparked interest in developing novel applications for them. A crucial aspect of these materials is their enhanced van der Waals forces, which significantly impact their electronic and thermal properties. Using first-principles calculations, we examined the thermodynamic and electronic behavior of two-dimensional MoS2 and WS2, considering both their closely packed and separated states. We observed a sudden change in the magnetic and caloric properties of MoS2 and WS2 when transitioning from isolated to packed states, with the closed MoS2 state exhibiting closeness-induced spin-polarized half-metallic character and large magnetocaloric effects induced by pressure at 0K and 300K.

This study investigates the impact of electron outflow and nonlocal effects on the resonance frequencies of gap-plasmons in metallic structures, specifically metallic strips with varying widths. To account for nonlocal responses, a extended version of the random phase approximation, where the electron outflow is described by a generalized Lindhard dielectric function, is utilized. Our results reveal that nonlocal effects and electron outflow significantly influence the resonance frequencies of gap-plasmons, especially at small widths. To a first-order approximation, we demonstrate that the generalized dielectric function enables precise predictions of resonance frequencies. When the width becomes very small, our theory predicts a shift in resonance frequencies to higher values and a complete suppression of resonance as the width approaches zero, due to significant electron outflow. These findings are validated by local DFT simulations, experimental data, and quasi-local time-dependent DFT.

A robust normalization process is proposed, resistant to syntactic transformations, for the Calculus of Constructions. Previously, robust normalization methods had been adapted for the Cumulative Calculus of Constructions, as seen in H. Bunderstein's research. Nevertheless, challenges persist in addressing non-cumulative constructions.

Recent advancements in condensed matter physics have sparked the use of mathematical abstractions, particularly topology, to understand complex quantum phenomena. This approach leverages significant computational resources available for simulating quantum systems. As topological quantum computing matures, employing real-world materials to implement quantum computations becomes a plausible approach. Utilizing the 1D Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model, we explored the conceptual underpinnings of topological quantum computations. Through the application of SSH Hamiltonians, we were able to circumvent the decoherence issues associated with complex interacting qubits, while still achieving a 95% success rate in preparing the target computational basis state. Furthermore, our research highlights the ability of simple models to demonstrate a previously unreported feature – a smooth transition between topological and non-topological phases within the SSH framework, which can be observed experimentally.

A new class of dependent Dirichlet processes has been introduced by West and Tawn (2006), now known as the Dirichlet process with stochastic weights (DPSW). Building on the work of West and Tawn, a broader category of processes has been defined by utilizing an exchangeable random measure as its foundation. The characteristics of these newly defined processes have been thoroughly examined, leading to the discovery of specific conditions that ensure these processes behave like standard Dirichlet processes. Furthermore, a method has been proposed to estimate the concentration parameter from a finite sample, as well as explore the processes' behavior in the context of spatial point processes, particularly in relation to the Poisson-Dirichlet process.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four gluons in QCD within a cavity, specifically for an odd-parity state with a large angular momentum, which behaves like a type Q supergravity state. By employing the BFKF-BK approach, we confirmed that the amplitude's behavior at leading order in the logarithmic term confirms the current understanding of the beta function's basis in QCD, which was previously thought to be resolved. However, at the next-order logarithmic term, the amplitude exhibits an ambiguity that originates from a mixture of missing contributions to the base in which the beta function is represented.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been limited by memory management issues due to premature saturation. Despite the object-based programming paradigm providing a familiar pattern for memory allocation and optimization, its performance benefits have not been fully realized on GPUs due to suboptimal data layout, which hinders memory access optimization. To address this limitation, a new data structure called DynaSOAr, a concurrent object-based memory allocator on GPUs, has been introduced. Built using the lock-free algorithm, DynaSOAr features an optimized slab allocator for lock management and a hash table for deferred list operations, allowing for high concurrency. Performance evaluations show that DynaSOAr outperforms existing high-concurrency allocators on GPUs by a significant margin in terms of maximum concurrent threads, allocation rates, and overall application performance.

This paper examines the boundedness of a broad class of operators, including fractional and Calderon-Zygmund singular integral operators, from generalized mixed Morrey spaces into their overlaps, and also investigates the boundedness of commutators by these operators.

Using a first-principles approach based on relativistic initial principles, we develop a comprehensive understanding of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (USR) effect for an electron spin triplet d-orbital Mn atom, considering both a single Mn atom and a pair of Mn atoms arranged end-to-end or side-by-side on the Nb(110) surface. Our analysis reveals that exchange and crystal electric fields overcome the Mn 3d electron's Coulomb repulsion, and that USR resonances exhibit a shift due to crystal electric field and exchange interaction. Furthermore, the resonance splitting observed in previous studies can be fully explained by the combined effects of crystal electric field and exchange interaction. The theoretical model provided can be easily fitted to experimental or first-principles data to determine the model's parameters.

Our proposed FourierMask achieves instance segmentation as an implicit function, utilizing FourierMapping to transform the parameterized coordinates of a 2D plane into values of the implicit function. By evaluating the values at coordinates corresponding to objects, we determine the structure of the target object. FourierMask is trained through a custom loss function in conjunction with Multi-scale Boundary Loss (MSBL), which accounts for the characteristics of object boundaries. It has been discovered that segments produced by FourierMask tend to concentrate on the edges of objects. By optimizing MSBL, we are able to enhance its ability to capture accurate boundaries. Trained independently of any specific image dimension or pixel style, FourierMask is capable of delivering highly precise mIO scores. When compared to previous implicit neural architecture models like ChanNet and NeRF-mask, FourierMask demonstrates superior performance on MSRA-Instance Segmentation and COCO datasets according to extensive experimental results.

This paper provides a topological framework for the configuration spaces of $m$ distinct points within the allowable confined configurations of $M$ within a smooth manifold of dimension $2n$, labeled $\mathcal{C}(M)$. The allowed confined configurations refer to the subset of the configuration space of $m$ distinct points within $M$, where $m$ does not include situations in which two points coincide at boundary points of $M$. This paper builds upon previously established results, specifically [11], by extending the understanding of $\mathcal{C}(M)$ for various types of confined configurations and providing new insights for a specific subclass of these configurations, denoted $\mathcal{C}'(M)$. The intrinsic confined configurations, denoted $\mathcal{C}'(M)$, are defined as the subset of $\mathcal{C}(M)$ where $m$ points contain at least one point located at the boundary of $M$ with an odd number of points. Our analysis of cloud data from multiple satellites reveals a discrepancy between cloud brightness at different wavelengths that cannot be explained by typical cloud properties. We explain this discrepancy as a result of upwelling radiation from within clouds, specifically due to large cloud droplets and warm surrounding surfaces. We explored how various factors influence this phenomenon and found it most pronounced in thick, convective clouds with large droplets. We developed a new classification system for clouds that incorporates this "veiled core" phenomenon. We predict that internal mixing of clouds may be useful for improving climate models by incorporating this factor.

To overcome the challenge of accessing high-energy particles for nuclear fusion, a transparent, relativistic skin depth barrier is proposed using an intensely short, chirped pulse. This proposed solution addresses limitations of prior methods by eliminating the need for precise peak power demands and instead prioritizing gradual, controlled changes in pulse characteristics to maintain efficiency. A newly developed, user-friendly simulation tool has been created to streamline the design process of these high-intensity pulses and facilitate exploration of various configurations to optimize performance in achieving nuclear fusion fuel access.

To determine whether terrestrial planets can sustain liquid water on their surfaces, astrophysicists conduct hydro-dynamic simulations of surrounding gases. These simulations consider the planets' masses, masses of their stars, and the planets' distances from their stars. Performing such simulations also predicts whether smaller gas giants or hybrid planets could sustain liquid water on their surfaces. However, no such habitable mini-Neptune has been observed thus far. We present TOI-712, an stellar system consisting of two transiting planets orbiting within or beyond their respective habitable zones. TOI-711b, characterized as a super-Euver or mini-Neptune with a minimum mass equivalent to eight Earth masses, is located within its habitable zone, while TOI-711c, identified as either a mini-Neptune or low-mass gas giant with a minimum mass equivalent to $7.7_{-2.8}^{+4.1}$ Mars masses, orbits beyond its habitable zone. TOI-711 has a youthful age of approximately 500 million years, as suggested by its overall properties.

A comprehensive, first-principles study has been performed to explore the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen within TiO2 in the rutile structure. Utilizing a range of computational methods, including RPBE, HSE06, and GW, we analyzed the impact of infusing C or N on TiO2's optical properties. Our results indicate that replacing O with C or N results in additional states within TiO2's optical gap. Specifically, N-infused TiO2 exhibits a reduction in optical gap size compared to O-infused TiO2, with the HSE06 method showing a VBM elevation and LBM descent. Furthermore, HSE06 computes the optical gap of N-rTiO2 to be 1.77eV, with both C and N acting as magnetic moments with values of 1.26$\mu_B$ and 1.64$\mu_B$ respectively.

This letter discusses the difficulty of producing top-quark pairs in central elastic scattering between protons, noting that traditional methods make this process practically impossible. However, an unorthodox approach called 'elastic creation' is proposed, in which individual top quarks are created elastically. This approach, though not entirely efficient, can make certain processes involving elastic scattering observable. If elastic creation does occur, it could provide a means of creating certain missing energy events that include top-quark signatures, providing a means of testing the Standard Model and exploring new physics beyond it.

The evaluation of atmospheric coherence structures is an established technique used to assess the complexity of turbulent flows. Its application within the cluster sector is also beneficial in understanding the intricate dynamics of intra-cluster turbulence. However, current coherence measurements are compromised by measurement inaccuracies which can distort the assessment of structural complexity. This paper first explains the relationship between coherence values and Correlation Dimension estimates, and derives a specific formula for this relation. As such, re-evaluation of previously estimated CD values is conducted using this newly derived relation. Moreover, accuracy thresholds for coherence measurements required for reliable CD estimation are determined. Finally, predictions are made regarding the feasibility of obtaining accurate CD estimates of turbulent scalars with next-generation adaptive optics systems using high-speed multi-channel detectors. This study is complemented by simulations of turbulent atmospheres at various resolution angles, flow rates and measurements of noise power spectra. In 1995, Erdos and Galvin conjectured that for any Ramsey coloring of the integers, there would be a monochromatic component in a specific monolithic set, with a density approaching one. This paper provides the first significant progression towards this conjecture by proving that for any monochromatic set, there is a monochromatic component with a density of at least $19/20 + \epsilon$. Additionally, it is shown that this bound can be approached closely, with a non-colorable graph with a density of $2-\delta$ found for any sufficiently small $\delta$. This graph can be Ramsey colored such that any 'red' or 'blue' subgraph will have a dense monochromatic component with a density of at least $2-\delta$.

At the heart of the Galactic Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), dense stellar aggregates show a surprising tendency for mass clusters to form elongated structures aligned with the long axis of the region.  Utilizing ATLAS and ATLAS III near-infrared astrometry and astrophotography, a novel statistical model was created to explore spatial arrangements of stellar clusters in greater detail.  This model calculates the probability of finding another stellar cluster within specified distances and angles from a focal point, revealing significant anisotropic patterns at intermediate scales (20-80 parsecs).  Aligned mostly with the long axis of the CMZ, these patterns are most obvious in the Southern hemisphere, particularly in sectors where negative gas velocity swirls.  These stellar cluster connections generally remain visible over 10 parsecs, but wider scales (up to 40 parsecs) in the Northern hemisphere display similar aligned patterns.  A statistical test known as the Rand index confirms that the observed clustering exceeds what might be expected by chance, and that a smaller dataset representing the Northern hemisphere exhibits comparable arrangement styles.  Furthermore, distinct differences emerged between stellar cluster arrangements in the inner and outer regions of the CMZ, with notable differences visible in cluster connectivity.  These findings have significant implications for understanding the dynamics and evolution of dense stellar clusters in the heart of our galaxy.

A significant portion of individuals affected by Bell's Palsy, an acute paralysis of the eye center, occur in patients under 40 years old.  Existing research focuses primarily on image processing to detect Bell's Palsy. In contrast, our work centers on analyzing video footage to identify patients affected by the condition. Our approach involves extracting frames from border and central locations, combining them into a singular composite image, and employing the MobileNet v1 network in conjunction with the Gradient Trust Region method to achieve a high level of accuracy (97.97%) in detecting Bell's Palsy while efficiently utilizing computational resources. Our model also demonstrates an ability to be effectively deployed on portable devices such as the Raspberry Pi 3.

In our analysis of quchutrit q-extended quantum electrodynamics, we found that its 2-site, four-body interactions disrupt the sound enhancement effect. Originally, the model exhibited local correlations decaying as $1/r$ due to sound velocities approaching zero, enabling it to demonstrate the model's hallmark characteristic. However, sound enhancements could also be observed in simplified models at sites separated by distances of $2$ or $3$ bond lengths. Consequently, measuring this effect requires comparing local correlations at such specific distances. Moreover, adding interaction between neighboring spins in the sQED model caused sound to spread over longer distances, making it ineffective to mitigate the noise on a local scale.

Research into highly polarized particles is valuable in advancing fundamental research and developing sensitive medical imaging techniques. To produce highly polarized particles, we need stable sources capable of generating them in bulk quantities. In this study, we investigated the emission of spin-polarized positrons during laser interactions with dense matter targets doped with fully polarized electrons. By using circularly and linearly polarized lasers in combination with various target configurations, we found that the highest positron polarization levels could be achieved with a high-polarization electron target illuminated by a high-polarization laser. This condition satisfies an equality between the rates of polarization gain and depolarization. As a temporary equilibrium, this results in the emission of positrons with significant levels of polarization. This research highlights the potential for producing highly polarized positron beams with significant applications in advanced medical diagnostics and radiopharmaceutical production.

This paper builds on a concept first introduced by R. I. Grigorieff in his 2000 study on limited groups. A group G, limited according to Grigorieff, is one where the inner automorphism group, denoted as Inner(G), is also limited. In this paper, we focus on identifying specific subclasses of groups where the inner automorphism group is limited, particularly those containing a given solvable length l and a maximal nilpotent derived subgroup. By extending previous work by G. A. Jones and W. P. Shemwell on groups of limited automorphisms, our results contribute to the broader objective of classifying groups with limited automorphisms by examining their composition factors. The theorems presented in this study provide a foundation for understanding groups with limited automorphisms by establishing relationships between a group's structure and its inner automorphism group.

A low-power temperature sensing interface has been developed, utilizing a bandgap-oriented technique and stored voltage differences.  This design is optimized for minimal power consumption in high-temperature scenarios and features a supply voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V.  A 12-bit $\Delta$-$\Sigma$ analog-to-digital converter transforms the temperature signal into a low-power output and achieves an 85dB signal-to-noise ratio.  With supply voltages between 0.6V and 1.2V, the transformer consumes as little as 0.37nW and can perform a transformation in 15ms.  A customized temperature sensor circuit, based on CTAT, PTAT, and bulk temperature-dependent phenomena, contributes minimally (0.3K) to the final measurement error due to its small common-mode range.  A calibration technique, leveraging the large AD conversion gain (3.5K) and high SNR, forms the basis of a highly precise temperature detection system with a standard deviation of 0.24$\deg$C.  In a 180nm CMOS process, three operational corners, and a variety of supply voltages and temperature conditions, the system exhibits an extremely small error variation (1.4$\deg$C) and a remarkably efficient energy per transformation (1.06nJ).

Recent observations of many T dwarfs and brown dwarfs have revealed strong magnetic fields maintaining axial symmetry. These fields seem unusually stable considering the inherent turbulent nature of stellar interiors where the fields are located. To better understand the persistence and structure of these fields, the characteristics of the surrounding environment, as well as the conditions under which they remain stable, must be explored through numerical modeling. A 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulation was conducted to examine the long-term behavior of strong axial magnetic fields in a star-like environment, using the PLIC-PIVOT code to analyze the fields' structure and stability over time. The findings showed that the fields persisted for an extended period, significantly reducing the fields to only 10% of their initial strength after an extended period, which corresponds to approximately 1.5 times the mixing time. The degree of reduction increased with the degree of turbulence induced by the velocity of the boundary. A theoretical framework was developed to understand the fields based on the balance between the magnetic tension and turbulent-induced decay, as well as the fields' spatial scale, which is maintained due to the magnetic tension overcoming convective turnover. The findings showed that the magnetic fields in axial symmetry share similarities with the magnetic fields observed in some stars, in particular those exhibiting active regions, despite the latter displaying higher degrees of overall activity.

In this work, we apply a specific numerical method to solve a class of dynamical field theory equations. Our approach converts the traditional differential-integral equations into a discrete equation form, making it easier to find a stable and accurate solution. The method relies on an iterative process to reach a solution that minimizes a given error function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method for a class of models whose behavior changes over time, and it may also be applicable to other complex systems involving time. A crucial aspect of this method is the use of an optimized basis function, and the success of the approach is now being tested on a class of $N$-component order parameter models.

A key advantage of our method is that it overcomes a common limitation in solving field theory equations related to causality constraints. We are able to disregard these constraints during the solution process and only apply them in a final optimization step to ensure a physically meaningful solution. We also introduce a new, more efficient way to handle the complex integro-differential equations by formulating them in a way that has multiple minimal solutions, and the unique, physically relevant solution can be found by applying the necessary criteria. This reformulation allows for a more efficient solution process and leads to a better understanding of the underlying physics.

Music information retrieval has traditionally relied on audio analysis and textual metadata, but a significant portion of modern music comprises non-lyriced vocals that can provide crucial context for listeners. This study introduces the "Pied Piper" dataset, comprising 45,000 text-based queries that span explicit, implicit, and context-dependent knowledge about 15,000 popular songs. It also presents context-aware relation detection between lyrics and metadata, along Parnassus, a comprehensive evaluation of music retrieval systems using real-world data.

This working paper builds key concepts from higher category theory, including fibration sequences, mapping cylinders, and path groupoids, within the context of Lie groupoids and stacks. We leverage these ideas to derive the standard fibration sequence for a fibration of Lie groupoids or stacks. Additionally, we provide an adjustable Lie groupoid or stack mapping cylinder, a relative path Lie groupoid, and a refined exact sequence that connects the homotopy types of a Lie groupoid, its associated space, and its relative path Lie groupoid.

Observations of a dragon infrared dark nebula in the Ophiuchus molecular cloud using ALMA and PanSTARRS2 have revealed an unseen massive star, M11, at its center. Alarmingly, this star is not radiating normally and appears to be rapidly expanding, or even losing mass at a core, which is highly abnormal for stars of its kind. Despite being surrounded by a dense gas cloud, star M11 has not formed a visible wind shock, further adding to the anomaly. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of massive star evolution and the conditions required for these stars to form.

Godel's modal logic extends classical modal reasoning by replacing binary relations with partial binary relations, or relations that don't apply to all input pairs. This paper explores algebraic and relational structures for various types of Godel's modal algebras and pre-algebras, including those based on many-valued relations. We analyze the corresponding algebraic and relational structures for these Godel modal systems.

LiDAR, or Light Detection and Ranging, utilizes laser technology to create 3D point clouds representing physical objects in their surrounding environment. These point clouds are instrumental in applications such as autonomous vehicles, spatial analysis, and forestry studies. However, there is currently a lack of standardization in how LiDAR datasets are processed, with numerous potential processes affecting final results. To address this issue, we propose a multi-level framework that classifies methods for manipulating LiDAR data, from basic descriptor creation to complex object and scene modeling. Furthermore, this framework can be applied to other types of intelligent data mining in point clouds.

Building advanced models for analyzing and predicting variables associated with the sphere requires an understanding of spectral representations and spatial correlation structures. These correlations can be simplified using conditional relationships, specifically when values of a stationary stochastic field on the sphere depend on values from adjacent regions. These 1-step relationships, when combined with non-negative covariance properties, facilitate the development of a spectral representation through a discrete measure defined over the set of spherical harmonic frequencies. This definition allows for the construction of spherical harmonic coefficients that are independent, complex Gaussian variables with zero mean and a common variance-bivariate covariance relationship, ultimately enabling the recovery of the original field through a expansion in terms of spherical harmonics. This development mirrors a previously established result for Euclidean spaces, and a preliminary application to data from SWEAP and SOLARIS missions on the Sun is presented.

The IceCube Neutrino Observatory in the Southern Hemisphere has the capability to investigate the source of neutrinos and other high-energy particles coming from outer space. In a new analysis, we examined the relationship between neutrinos and cosmic rays in energy levels above 185 EeV, focusing on whether their arrival directions correlated with known sources of extragalactic radiation or large galaxies within 150 megaparsecs. Our results showed no significant correlations in the northern sky, while a slight correlation was found in the southern sky, although this result lacks statistical significance. Our data also revealed that the flux of neutrinos and cosmic rays, when compared, increased at a similar rate, which is consistent with a diffuse background rather than point sources.

We observe a notable rise in foam resistivity as thickness decreases, a phenomenon we attribute to surface roughness induced tilt resistance. A mathematical model is developed to incorporate the effects of boundary-induced variations in the mean curvature of the interface, and we demonstrate that a two-dimensional foam's resistance follows an $H/12\pi$ pattern in the thin-layer limit, where $H$ represents the mean curvature. Furthermore, our findings indicate that three-dimensional foam resistance scales according to the inverse of the mean curvature.

Approximately 3 million new skin cancer cases are diagnosed annually, making it the most prevalent type of cancer. Due to the diverse appearance of skin cancers and the difficulty in distinguishing malignant moles from benign ones, distinguishing between these types can be challenging. To automate this process, computer-aided diagnosis systems analyze images of skin cancers. While researchers have made significant strides in creating accurate classification models using manual feature extraction, this approach requires extensive work to identify suitable features. In contrast, the method proposed here employs a CNN to automatically extract features and incorporates a Disorder to Identify Outlier samples (DISO) approach to detect and address outlier images that do not conform to the expected pattern. The combination of CNN and DISO results in improved performance in distinguishing between malignant moles and dermatosis images, as evidenced by results from multiple datasets, including three classes, twelve classes, and a challenging dataset consisting of two classes with enhanced balance.

We investigated a viscous fluid being steadily poured into a spinning Hele-Shaw cell and observed flexible fingers made of membrane made it possible to observe the patterns formed by the fluid. By utilizing numerical modeling, we took into account the effect of the cell's angular velocity on the number of formed modes, where an increase in angular velocity led to a more compact arrangement of the modes due to the Coriolis force causing them to spiral. The number of modes remained unaffected by the cell's rotation, yet their arrangement changed. In areas away from the center, higher stresses caused by the centrifugal force led to more pronounced walls in the formed modes. The interaction between the centrifugal and Coriolis forces also led to a more balanced wall thickness in some places. The study of heating the fluid revealed that it led to convection rolls forming due to the hotter fluid rising, leading to the creation of spiral patterns due to the cell's rotation. The stability of these patterns was influenced by how quickly the membrane cooled down, with a balance being reached in some cases.

Spectroscopic data from the dark cloud TMC-1 revealed two identical but structurally distinct molecules ethynyl cyclopentadiene and ethynyl cyclopentadiene with the same chemical formula. Using a combined analysis of spectral data, a model was created to determine the abundance of these molecules to be approximately 10^-9 relative to H2 for both isomers. The formation of complex cyclic molecules like these can be attributed to the presence of smaller hydrocarbon cycles such as cyclobutadiene, cyclooctatetraene, benzene, and naphthalene, which have estimated fractional abundances relative to H2 of 10^-11, 10^-10, 10^-10, and 10^-10 respectively. The actual quantities of these molecules are likely higher as previous studies have found indications of benzene and naphthalene in the interstellar medium. The formation of ethynyl cyclopentadiene can also be explained by a third cyclic molecule consisting of five carbon atoms and four hydrogen atoms.

This paper introduces the focus model in Look-ahead Focus Creation (LFoCuS), a paradigm for explaining high-dimensional structures in Look-ahead Focus (LF) models. Specifically, it argues that focusing models must consider how changes to a model affect its ability to make accurate predictions. Conversely, the focus creation aspect deals with how modifying the distribution of attention within the model can simplify and make it more interpretable. The method introduced uses a technique called L-shaped Valley (LValley) Descent to transform complex structures into simpler ones, making them easier to interpret and align with human understanding. The proposed approach is evaluated using several real-world datasets, including explanations for gene networks, plant disease predictions, and weather clearance assessments, demonstrating its effectiveness through combined results from existing and novel methods. The code is available for use at the provided URL.

Over recent decades, a shift has occurred in how scientists conduct research, with large-scale projects requiring significant financial investment to be executed. Consequentially, major scientific endeavors have started collaborating to utilize shared resources, ultimately giving rise to grid computing. This concept emerged from attempting to combine previously independent computing systems across diverse organizations and geographical locations. To achieve this collaboration, a translational approach was adopted, involving the creation of shared protocols and methodologies that could be translated between different computing environments. This translation process facilitated the combination of these disparate systems, contributing to the development of grid computing.

A new form of cosmological model, known as 'fluid of the century,' has the potential to describe both dark energy and matter in a unified concept, suggesting they may be interconnected and subject to viscous forces. The study combines multiple relativistic concepts, including viscoelasticity, the first law of thermodynamics, and the conservation of mass, to develop a model that reflects the interdependence of dark energy and matter. The resulting solutions to the model's elasticity parameters reveal that the model's components exhibit oscillatory behavior, with the mean values of its density showing convergence to the observed values from the $\Lambda$CDM model in the distant past. Furthermore, the Hubble parameter's present-day values are found to be consistent with the observed data. In addition, the model's present-day deceleration parameter is found to be in agreement with the accelerating expansion of the cosmos. A key finding of the study is that the model's present-day values for its state equation parameter are influenced by the model's viscosity and elasticity, with the values ultimately being in alignment with the observed data. Overall, the research provides a comprehensive framework for the interconnection of dark energy and matter, and its implications are further explored through the use of the Weizs\"acker plot and other parameters.

In contemporary society, fostering life-long learning and a positive attitude towards knowledge acquisition are considered essential, as they lay the groundwork for lifelong success, with curiosity playing a crucial role in this process, with a positive attitude towards learning serving as a precursor to effective knowledge acquisition. Unfortunately, accurately assessing a learner's internal cognitive emotional state from external behavioral patterns within a learning environment remains a complex challenge due to the variability and subtlety of nonverbal expressions of curiosity. To address this problem, we present a original approach to analyzing facial expressions, verbal interactions, and contextual cues to gauge a learner's level of curiosity while they engage in collaborative learning. By leveraging a combination of explicit assessments, implicit indicators, and data from video and audio recordings, we developed a comprehensive model that uses a weighted ensemble of machine learning algorithms to accurately predict a learner's curiosity levels. Our approach, which integrates the strengths of various techniques while minimizing their respective weaknesses, was tested and demonstrated a higher effectiveness than competing methods. Our research also highlights the potential for using our approach to inform the design of more effective learning experiences, as we uncover the unique characteristics of curiosity in real-world settings and the implications for the development of more efficient and reliable techniques for analyzing emotional states in educational environments. Ultimately, we believe that our approach paves the way for the advancement of emotionally intelligent multimodal systems that can effectively assess and respond to a wide range of emotional states in complex learning settings.

Recently, random fields following Mat\'ern correlations have gained significant interest in geostatistics and spatial statistics, particularly where data points are located at irregular positions. These functions have also been adapted for use on graphs. A newer class of functions that incorporate \alpha-smoothness and \beta-growth parameters has been introduced for both irregular settings and graph-based settings. We demonstrate the feasibility of utilizing these functions for regression tasks through a suboptimal regression algorithm introduced for graph-based settings. A theoretical analysis of the algorithm's properties has been conducted, along with empirical evaluations using synthetic and real-world data sets that include a 2D real estate example and a mouse brain connectivity matrix. Results using the Mat\'ern graph regression algorithm have outperformed Gaussian Process Regression and the Graph Laplacian smoother in terms of reduced prediction error. Additional advantages of the algorithm include its transparency, scalability, and adaptability to diverse applications, making it a promising tool for efficient and interpretable multi-node data smoothing.

Metropolis road networks can be effectively monitored using a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles equipped with sensors, taking advantage of the fact that they traverse significant portions of the network.

A new framework is proposed to solve the problem of road network observation, where the goal is to develop an optimal strategy for a fleet of mobile sensors to monitor a metropolitan road system, considering that sensors can initiate missions from any point within the system.

An evaluation method is created to assess the effectiveness of different sensor deployment methods by calculating their ability to cover the road system, and a efficient algorithm is developed to determine the best possible outcome for any given situation.

Numerical results show that specific strategies, such as having sensors use the road system's main paths or any random strategy, are less effective than optimal approaches, with metropolis road systems presenting a unique and challenging observation problem that differs from previous studies on sensor deployment.

Most stable implicit methods for handling stiff differential equations fixed their time step size, a common approach that worked well before. During time integration, researchers could efficiently balance accuracy and computational cost by adjusting the fixed step size. However, fixing the time step size had a problematic effect on the degree of the method. As the time step size changed, this balance would influence the optimal method degree. This negative consequence was unresolved until fixed coefficient methods were created, which maintained an optimal method degree despite varying time step sizes. This paper builds variable time step implicit single step methods for standard applications by combining a modified Kutta approach with exponential time differentiation formulas. These new methods can switch between method degrees and time step sizes to achieve an effective efficiency that competes with the conventional practice. Two distinctive properties emerged from this research. First, simplified proofs were achieved for proving methods stability and convergence. Second, this research discovered that not all optimal method coefficients could be found using rational approximation techniques. To demonstrate this, the paper includes an example where such methods cannot be constructed. This research extends a previous study by relaxing assumptions about the underlying functions these methods process. This research extends another study by showing compatibility with text-based initial value problems. Furthermore, this research introduces a new efficiency metric suitable for comparing the efficiency of fixed and variable time step methods. Two case studies were used to show that methods with fixed time step sizes and optimal method coefficients perform equally to their variable time step counterparts.

In recent years, analyzing large-scale functional time series has gained significant attention in statistics and economics research. Although various analytical techniques have been developed, most assume a fixed number of functional components. Our proposed method, MfSSE, addresses this limitation by evaluating the effective dimensionality of a large functional time series dataset without assuming a fixed number of underlying components. Much like its univariate counterpart, MfSSE employs a reconstruction error approach to identify the number of underlying components and a clustering strategy to evaluate the quality of the resulting components. We evaluate the performance of MfSSE through both artificial and real-world data sets.
